A very good morning to everybody. Secretary General of the United Nations, Heads of State, President of Spain, Vice Presidents, Prime Ministers and representatives of international organisations and multilateral organisations, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, The Queen and I would like to welcome you to Spain, to Andalusia, to Seville, for this fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. This city, which is open to the world, a city that is both Mediterranean and Atlantic, which is both European and Ibero-American, welcomes you with open arms because this city is aware, as are all Spaniards, of the great significance of the message that must emanate from this summit, a renewed and fresh impetus for the sustainable development agenda. Spain is proud of having been chosen to be the host. which reflects our journey and growing commitment to multilateralism and international cooperation over the last four decades. Seville, the first European city to host this summit, follows Monterrey, Doha and Addis Ababa as a meeting point for us to discuss a crucial question: how to strengthen the framework for financing for development at this highly complex time. I hope that your voice will resound loud and clear, that a new roadmap will emanate from this summit, one that is based on what is concrete and tangible and actionable, because in these times, delivering on our commitment is the best way to reach the entire international community. Ladies and gentlemen, distinguished delegates, this conference must be a success because international cooperation is one of the fundamental pillars of the multilateral world. It is the ultimate embodiment of the values that sustain it, especially at this particular point in history where many certainties are melting away and many fears and uncertainties are taking shape. I would like to take the opportunity of being here to underscore three ideas. Firstly, in an ever-changing world, cooperation must serve to build the future for generations to come, but also it reflects a present of which we are all, the international community, part of and responsible for. Because there is only one reality and it cannot be fragmented. It doesn't work in silos. And in this context, the sustainable development agenda adopted in 2015, and now we are five years away from the deadline we set ourselves for its achievement, remains fully relevant because global challenges cannot be deferred. They require fresh momentum for our collective effort. And the time has come to give ourselves that energy with determination, with effectiveness and with guarantees of shared responsibility. The second idea that I'd like to mention is that at a time in which the challenges stand very tall and when there is a clear lack of financing, the only possible response is that of efficiency. The language of efficiency is the language that must define this conference, the language that will be found in the outcome document in the Seville commitment, which is the fruit of a consensus which in and of itself is a great cause for celebration. And it is also the language that will shine through in the Seville platform for action, a platform designed for weaving partnerships and mobilizing resources around the sustainable development goals. Your work and your ability to build virtuous circles and levers for development and prosperity will be the best possible defense for multilateralism. My third point is that the tremendous shifts that we are living through, heading towards a new form of geopolitics, cannot and must not lead to a total revision of the the rule of law, of solidarity, of human dignity of the world, which is to be found in the Universal Declaration on Human Rights and the UN Charter. We must be very careful to ensure that that does not happen. Despite the difficulties, we must continue on the long path of multilateral diplomacy, not because we believe that that is always the most direct or swiftest path, or because we refuse to see its clear shortcomings, but rather because we know where other paths have led throughout history. The United Nations and its specialized agencies and bodies must continue to play a central role as the main source of stimulus for so many processes of dialogue and cooperation. Speakers, distinguished delegates, as Dag Hammarskjold said, the Secretary General of the United Nations between 1953 and 1961, and one of the most clear-sighted diplomats of the 20th century, said, "The pursuit of peace and progress cannot end in a few years in either victory or defeat. The pursuit of peace and progress, with its trials and its errors, its successes and its setbacks, can never be relaxed and never abandoned. So let us continue this pursuit. Let us make the Seville Conference a new milestone on the agenda for development. We owe it to the generation of our forefathers, and we also owe it to the generation of our children and grandchildren, and we owe it to all those who, in our own time, have not the voice or the energy with which to call for a better and fairer world. For them, for us, sustainable development is a cause that we must never renounce. Thank you very much, and I wish you every success.

In 2015, the global community came together to set a bold plan for people and planet. Yet today, the Sustainable Development Goals are off track, and the financing gap to meet the goals has soared. In Seville, our challenge is to renew commitment to financing the agenda so that countries are empowered to leverage resources to fund education, health, and other essential services for all. So that private capital is unlocked to invest in opportunities across all countries at scale. For international development cooperation that finances for maximum impact crowds in resources and builds global solidarity. For international trade that spurs development, creating jobs and sharing knowledge. For a debt framework that delivers for development, lowering borrowing costs and resolving debt crises effectively and fairly. For a reformed international financial architecture that is inclusive and better protects countries from shocks and crises. and for a world where science, technology and innovation work to solve our biggest challenges. This is the moment to renew the spirit and hope of the SDGs, to build unity, to turn commitments into action. For people, for the planet and for generations to come.

Distinguished heads of state and government, Your Majesty, the King of Spain, Your Majesty the Queen of Spain, Your Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Your Excellency Firimion Yang, President of the 79th Session of the General Assembly, Your Excellency Bob Rae, President of the Economic and Social Council, Ministers, Excellencies, distinguished participants. Therefore, Excellencies, the Government of Spain believes that this summit is an opportunity for us to change course, for us to raise our voice in the face of those who seek to convince us that rivalry and competition will set the tone for humanity and for its future. And that is why I suggest we focus on three goals. First of all, to turn our words into action. The Seville commitment should renew and take the legacy of Addis Ababa further. Therefore, it is essential to reform international financial architecture so as to make it more representative, more just and, above all, more effective. Thirdly, we have to bolster trust. We have to keep the flame alive and believe in it. In an ever more fragmented world, inclusive and strengthened multilateralism is more necessary than ever, and it must have the UN at its heart. A dialogue based on respect and where everybody is on equal footing should guide our decisions. There is no north and no south, there is just one humanity that requires joint solutions for joint challenges. Therefore, I would like to make the case for empathy, a quality that is inherent in multilateralism and which enables us to see the world from the other person's point of view. Let us Look beyond the random scars of history that we call borders, and let us see and act beyond our passports, because there is no border, however fortified, there is no wall, however high, that can slow down the challenges that we are facing. But let me assure you that nor can walls and borders slow down our commitment towards humanity and the planet. To conclude, I would like to sincerely thank all delegations for their work in this process, and in particular, I would like to praise the excellent work of the co-presidents, Portugal and Burundi, and that of the co-facilitators, Norway, Mexico, Zambia, and Nepal. Let us shine the bright light of beautiful Seville on the future of the generations that are to come. Thank you. Thank you very much. Your Majesties, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I thank the government and people of Spain for their warm welcome for us here in Seville for this important conference. For decades, the mission of sustainable development has united countries large and small, developed and developing. Together, we achieved progress, reducing global poverty and hunger, saving lives with stronger healthcare systems, getting more children into school, expanding opportunities for women and girls, and strengthening social safety nets. But today, development and its great enabler, international cooperation, are facing massive headwinds. We are living in a world where trust is fraying and multilateralism is strained. A world with a slowing economy, rising trade tensions, and decimated aid budgets. A world shaken by inequalities, climate chaos, and raging conflicts. The link between peace and development is clear. Nine of the 10 countries with the lowest human development indicators are currently in a state of conflict. Excellencies, financing is the engine of development. And right now, this engine is sputtering. As we meet, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development Our global promise to transform our world for a better, fairer future is in danger. Two-thirds of the Sustainable Development Goals targets are lagging. Achieving them requires an investment of more than $4 trillion a year. But this is not just a crisis of numbers. It's a crisis of people, of families going hungry, of children going unvaccinated, of girls forced to drop out of school. And we are here in Seville to change course, to repair and rev up the engine of development, to accelerate investment at the scale and speed required. and to restore a measure of fairness and justice for all.

Excellencies, the Seville commitment is a global promise to fix how the world supports countries as they climb the development ladder. I see three areas of action. First, we must get resources flowing fast. Countries must lead by mobilizing domestic resources and investing in areas of greatest impact schools, healthcare, social protection, decent work and renewable energy. Unlocking these investments requires strengthening tax systems and tackling illicit financial flows and tax evasion, and helping developing countries dedicate a greater share of their tax revenue to the systems people need. The Seville commitment calls on developed countries to double their aid dedicated to domestic resources mobilizations to support this. Multilateral and national development banks must unite to finance major investments. And this includes tripling the lending capacity of multilateral development banks and rechanneling special drawing rights that can unlock lending capacity and help developing countries boost investments. We also need innovative funding solutions to unlock private capital solutions that mitigate currency risks, that combine public and private finance more effectively and ensure the risks and rewards of development projects are shared by both the public and the private sectors, and that ensure financial regulations assess risk appropriately, and support investments in frontier markets. Second, we must fix the global debt system, which is unsustainable, unfair, and unaffordable. With annual debt service of US$1.4 trillion, countries need and deserve a system that lowers borrowing costs, enables fair and timely debt restructuring, and prevents debt crises in the first place. The Seville commitment lays the groundwork with other aspects, by also creating a single debt registry for transparency and promoting responsible lending and borrowing, by lowering the cost of capital through debt swaps and debt management support, and through debt service pauses in times of emergency, and third, We must increase the participation of developing countries in the institutions of the global financial architecture. The present major shareholders have a role to play, recognizing the importance of correcting injustices and adapting to a changing world. A new borrowers forum will give voice to borrowers for failure debt resolution and fairer gap resolution and to foster transparency, shared learning and coordinated debt action. And we need a fairer global tax system shaped by all, not just by a few.

Excellences, ladies and gentlemen, This conference is not about charity. It is about restoring justice and to facilitate the ability of all people to live in dignity. This conference is not about money. It is about investments in the future that we wish to build together. Thank you all for being a part of this important and ambitious effort.

Global financing needs have grown dramatically since 2015. This is especially true for developing countries which require 4.2 trillion dollars annually to close the financing gap. We must strengthen the voice and representation of developing countries not as beneficiaries, but as equal partners in shaping their destinies and in shaping our future. Your Excellencies, it is time to keep our promises. Let us ensure that Seville is remembered for what was set in motion, collective action to provide additional, innovative, adequate, affordable, predictable and accessible financing for development from all sources, including the private sector. Your Majesties, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, friends, it's an honour to welcome you to the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. We are meeting in in Seville at a critical time, full of possibilities but also responsibilities. Around the world, political priorities are changing. Trade barriers are increasing and international aid is shrinking. In this dynamic context, Our shared commitment to multilateralism and sustainable development has never been so important. That is why we are gathered here today to reaffirm our commitments and to set out our collective future. to overcome the fractures within our global financial system, to equip ourselves with the tools that will allow us better to respond to the challenges of today and to meet the needs of tomorrow, and to build a new path that is fair, inclusive and sustainable. This is a unique opportunity for us to remodel and improve the global financial architecture.

My friends, the stakes could hardly be higher. Financing needs for sustainable development have increased dramatically, and we have all an obligation to work collectively to be able to successfully respond to these critical needs. Climate finance is critical to address mitigation and adaptation needs of countries. We need tangible progress for the most vulnerable. It was a wise person who once pointed out that strategy without resources is better called hallucination. We have come a long way. Since the end of the Second World War, the 80 years that we are now recognizing today as a key anniversary for the United Nations, let us at least recognize that the global economy has been transformed, that billions have been lifted out of poverty, that we have in fact seen a tremendous increase in living standards in education and healthcare across the world. This progress does not only come from international institutions like the UN, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, but also from critical national and local efforts, what we call mobilizing domestic resources. This is what has helped to build the world we now live. It comes from not just governments, it comes from civil society, it comes from companies, and workers who are creating wealth in partnership. Financial system that serves humanity, it sounds like an impossible task, but in fact it can be done. But let me suggest a simple formula that the future is not inherited. I would like to thank the President of the Economic and Social Council for his statement. I now invite Mr. Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank Group, to address the conference.

Your Majesties, President Sanchez, Secretary General Guterres, distinguished guests, I think we are at an inflection point for development. On the one hand, we have the familiar challenges of poverty and fragility and conflict and rising debt and the need to build climate resiliency into everything that we do. Remember, ending poverty and a livable planet, as you saw in the opening video, is the mission of the World Bank Group. But on the other, there is a fast approaching demographic surge in emerging markets. I think that presents a huge opportunity for our future. But it doesn't really happen if these young people have access to clean air and clean water and education and health when they're growing up and when they're ready, the chance to have a job. And I think that challenge will require resources at an unprecedented scale and pace. We know that there isn't enough money in government, in philanthropies, or in development institutions to meet every projection or every promise. And that's why we need the private sector. It's also why we must be more strategic and change how each of us approaches this issue. So let me start with what I do with the World Bank Group. We've been asked to move faster, simplify, operate more efficiently, deliver more impact. What we've tried to do over the last couple of years is respond with a set of reforms aimed at one simple goal. that is the word that Bob used, be a better partner to our private sector and government clients. So for example, we've cut project approval times by a third from 19 to 13 months with some projects now getting approved in under 30 days. We've helped to deepen collaboration across the MDBs and DFI system. We've given clients a single point of contact by merging all our structures in 40 countries already with more to come. We have replaced 153 items scorecard with 22 outcome focused metrics, and we've sort of shaped our ambition around some very clear goals, connect 1.5 billion to primary healthcare, for example, or deliver capital to 80 million women to open businesses, or double the agribusiness financing we do to 9 billion a year, all the idea is to build ecosystems of growth. Last year, we put 133 billion dollars to work, plus mobilized another 66 billion of private capital. And with the new instruments and capital efficiency measures, we can expand our lending capacity by another 100 billion over the decade. The point is, this is all inadequate compared to the numbers you hear for the promises we need to deliver. Even our IDA 21 replenishment campaign, for which I thank many of you in the audience, including the government of Spain for their generosity. Even that replenishment campaign, which put together with our leverage capacity allows us to raise $100 billion for the next three years, 70% of which will go to Africa, even that at the end of the day is inadequate when you add the challenges and the money that needs to be put to work. Now, there's many ways to tackle this. We're not all just stuck. So for governments, the starting point is spending better. In developing countries, if they raise their revenues, as I think Antonio mentioned, domestic resource mobilization, if they raise their revenues to 15% of GDP, they could unlock 400 billion annually. In partnership with the IMF and Nigel is here, we're helping them get there, and then we assist them with budget reviews, cutting what doesn't work, shift spending to what does. We've already done this for 13 countries, we're in the process of bringing it for 11 more. What happens when you're doing these reviews is you discover hidden potential, like the $1.25 trillion every year that is spent on subsidies for agriculture, fisheries, and fossil fuels around the world. Don't get me wrong, some of those are necessary, but many are inefficient. You repurpose a portion and you could free up funds while still protecting the vulnerable. Such actions can take us far, but we need the private sector and the jobs they create, because jobs are the surest way to put a nail in the coffin of poverty. But the private sector cannot succeed alone. Our communal efforts are needed to create the right conditions, and I put those in three pillars. The first is essential infrastructure, both physical roads, ports, water, power and human healthcare, education and skills, each with resiliency built into it. Second, a business friendly environment, clear laws, transparent institutions. Third, support to scale for the private sector through capital and tools that reward risk taking and the sharing of the returns between the public and the private. I think the bank delivers all of these, we operate across the continuum of public financing, knowledge and private sector tools. What we're trying to do is focus on five sectors that generate local job creation. These are not sectors that are dependent on outsourcing from the developed economies. And that's infrastructure, physical and human, agribusiness, healthcare, tourism and local value added manufacturing. The potential of these sectors will only be realized if capital flows. Private investors don't fund good intentions. They fund opportunity and they go where there is a probability of return. I was in the private sector for 40 years. I learned one thing, a probability of return with a management of risk and I'll put my money to work. Over five years, The World Bank Group has provided $560 billion in financing the last five. We've mobilized $200 billion in private capital. And what doesn't get counted, we've also raised $250 billion from investors through bonds. The point is, it's still not enough. That's why we brought work with the private sector through the lab that actually Mark Carney and Srithi Vedera ran for us until Mark moved on to a somewhat more important role. And we're now deploying So practical tools to overcome each of these. The first, regulatory policy certainty. We're helping governments create investable environments. We're proving that it works through the energy compacts we're doing right now with a number of governments in Africa, many of whom are here in this room. They're committing to regulatory reforms. The idea is to advance our goal of providing electricity to 300 million people by 2030 in partnership with the African Development Bank. Second, political risk insurance. Even if you get this regulatory policy, the private investor needs this kind of insurance. We've streamlined our guarantees. Early signs, both in volume and client feedback, are very promising. Third, foreign exchange. Volatility will deter long-term investing. So one third of IRC's long-term commitments now in local currency, and we're headed to a target of 40% by 2030. Fourth, junior equity capital. We have launched the Frontier Opportunities Fund, this is a vehicle we have seeded with $100 million of IFC's income currently, we plan to do that every year, the idea is to absorb first loss risk, it's built to grow through donor and philanthropic contributions. And last, securitization, where we're working with global financial partners to standardize and package our loan portfolios and those of our brothers in the other MDBs, making it easier for large institutional investors to come into the emerging markets. Each of these efforts, the purpose is lower barriers that keep capital on the sidelines. But the real measure of success is not capital, it's whether we make a difference in people's lives. There is no greater difference than helping a person find dignity and find hope, and that only comes with a job. A friend of mine once said, poverty is a state of being and a state of mind. The being you can tackle with the earnings from a job. The mind is the dignity that a job gives you every day. By 2050, more than 80% of the world's population will live in countries we now call developing. In just the next decade, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in these countries, and they will be competing for only 400 million jobs that are likely to be created. That's a gap of 800 million. This generation has the collective power to shape the course of humanity for the next century. The question is, does that power ignite or does it impede? And that will depend on the choices we make at events like this. We have the opportunity. Do we have the will to create the conditions for jobs and unlock a generation's potential? That's the dedication that you'll find us at the World Bank moving towards. Thank you very much, sir.
I thank the President of the World Bank Group for his statement. I now invite Ms. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organization, to address the conference.

Your Majesty, the King of Spain, President Pedro Sanchez, Secretary-General Guterres, President of the General Assembly and President of ECOSOC, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for inviting the World Trade Organization to address this conference. I don't think that a conference has ever gathered in such difficult times, difficult for the world, for our shared development aspirations, and for the means to finance the attainment of these aspirations. After decades of positive contributions, which I must remind you, increased incomes in rich countries, and lifted 1.5 billion people out of poverty in the developing world, the global trading system has now been severely disrupted. Developing countries that had been hoping to increase export revenues to help prevent deterioration in their balance of payments must now contend with disruptions so considerable that they are feeding into financial instability. Amid unilateral tariff measures and record levels of policy uncertainty, at the WTO we have sharply downgraded our forecasts for the year. Instead of growing by 2.7%, almost 3% in 2025, we currently estimate that global merchandise trade volumes will basically be flat, growing at only 0.1%. The introduction or reintroduction of further tariff barriers on July 9th, would make the contraction worse. This is why we have argued that least developed countries as a group and Africa as a region should be exempted from these reciprocal tariffs so we can better integrate them into the world trading system, not further exclude them, so that they can stand a better chance to earn the resources with which to deliver on the sustainable development goals. So where do we go from here? The outcome document, Compromiso de Sevilla, rightly recognizes international trade as an engine for development. It is through trade that you can help earn your own domestic resources to finance your development. We therefore need to bolster stability and predictability in global trade. This involves action at multiple levels. First, we need to shore up the 74% of global goods trade that continues to cross borders on the basis of the WTO's most favored nation tariffs. And we need to ensure more countries can seize exciting opportunities to earn more resources to finance themselves through services, digital, green, and blue trade. Second, We believe that cooperative solutions to existing trade problems, not unilateral approaches, are the best way to go. But at the same time, we need to ask ourselves, how did we get here? And we need to respond to legitimate criticisms by the United States, the European Union, developing countries and others. that have been raised by trying to listen to these criticisms and reform and reposition the World Trade Organization. We must not waste this crisis if the WTO is to continue to offer a good value proposition for its members. Ministers must step up at the upcoming 14th Ministerial Conference in Cameroon and embrace and push forward the necessary reforms. We need to complement these multilateral reforms by also stepping up ongoing economic integration at the regional level in Europe, in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Most regional agreements are built on the WTO platform and complement the WTO, deepening them with strengthened international trade architecture and foster greater certainty in trade. Third, to unlock trade, we need to unlock and leverage investment and trade finance. As the outcome document recognises, attracting domestic and foreign investment to countries and communities on the margins of the global economy is vital to make growth inclusive. At the WTO, we are poised to contribute positively to this agenda with our new plurilateral instrument for investment facilitation for development, which will complement all the things that Ajit said they are doing at the World Bank. Fourth, we need to reduce trade finance gaps in developing countries. This would help accelerate trade and improve countries' fiscal positions. Our studies with the International Finance Corporation show that only 10 to 25% of goods trade is financed in many developing countries. Doubling this coverage would boost trade flows by an estimated 8% per year on average and allow countries to earn more of their own domestic resources. Fifth and finally, at this World Financing for Development Conference with so many leaders present, I must reiterate what Ajay Banga said. I want to emphasize once again that we have large amounts of financing locked up in harmful subsidies, which we should seek to repurpose. He mentioned $1.2 trillion. Actually, if you add some of the ones on agriculture and water and fisheries, harmful fisheries subsidies, we have almost $2 trillion locked up in subsidies that are doing more harm than good. Recognising the political difficulties involved in phasing out subsidies, I know this is not easy, I would just point out that if we can repurpose one-third to one-half of this, we would have much of the resources we need to address the problems that we are tackling for the sustainable development goals. At the WTO, we have done our part. We have delivered on SDG 14.6 on phasing out $22 billion in harmful fishery subsidies that lead to illegal, unregulated and unreported fishing of our oceans. 102 countries have ratified this agreement so far. We need only nine more for it to come into effect. So if your country has not ratified, please do so immediately so we can fully deliver on this SDG. In conclusion, Excellencies, yes, we are in difficult times and we face tough constraints, but we still have room to act at home and with each other to put sustainable development and financing back on track. A reformed multilateral trading system is certainly poised and willing to do its part. Thank you.
I thank the Director-General of the World Trade Organization for her statement. I now invite Mr. Nigel Clarke, Deputy Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, to address the conference.

Your Majesties, the King and Queen of Spain, President of the conference, Prime Minister Sanchez, United Nations Secretary General Guterres, President of the General Assembly, President of ECOSAC, Excellencies and authorities, good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today on behalf of the International Monetary Fund. It's a great honor to join you at this, the fourth Financing for Development Conference. This conference comes at a particularly challenging time. Once again, the resilience of the world economy is being tested. Uncertainty is escalating as major policy shifts reshape countries' priorities. And despite progress that has been made on trade talks and the scaling back of some tariffs, Trade policy uncertainty indicators are off the charts. This has major implications for developing countries for whom risks have grown, risks to short term and long term growth, risks of tightened financing conditions. and, yes, risks to their development agenda, including due to cuts in overseas development assistance. This is why this conference is so important and so timely. It provides an opportunity to take decisive and necessary steps to accelerate development progress. And these steps must be taken both at the individual country level but also at the international community level. With that in mind and with this opportunity in our hands, let me stress three critical priorities, one at the country level and two at the international level. First priority at the country level, implement strong domestic reforms. In an uncertain economic environment, the work to advance development must begin at home. And let me point to two sets of critical reforms within this first priority. First, domestic revenues remain the bedrock of country-led efforts for sustainable growth and development. Many countries can boost resources available to them by broadening the tax base and improving compliance. And secondly, by building strong public financial management systems, they can redirect spending to sectors like health and education and well-targeted social safety nets and growth enhancing public investments. second priority at the international level, ensure that support is coordinated and tailored. Development partners must help with policy advice, capacity building, and financial support. And to be effective, assistance should be tailored to countries' individual circumstances and challenges. Indeed, while developing economies have many characteristics in common, there are keen differences in their economic conditions. The needs of the poorest and most fragile countries in particular, who are often the hardest hit by global shocks, demand our attention. And for those countries, concessional financing remains of critical importance. The third priority, also at the international level, address debt vulnerabilities. The risk of systemic debt crisis seems broadly contained for now. But many countries continue to struggle with high interest costs and refinancing needs that constrain their ability to finance critical development spending and build resilience. This is why the international community must further improve debt restructuring processes to ensure that countries with unsustainable debt have access to timely and sufficiently deep debt relief. We have already seen progress under the common framework and at the global sovereign debt restructuring roundtable. And the recently published Sovereign Debt Restructuring Playbook is an important resource for countries considering a restructuring. But, Excellencies, there is still much more work to do. The IMF is doing its part in supporting developing countries. Through our tailored policy advice, we help our members make their economies more vibrant and more resilient. And we will continue to strengthen our analysis and guidance on monetary, fiscal, exchange rate, and financial sector policies. Through our capacity development, we'll continue to help equip our members with tools and expertise to chart their own path, working in close collaboration with development partners. Through our lending instruments, we provide financial support to our members when they need it most. Last fall, we reformed our concessional lending framework to double its lending capacity while restoring its self-sustainability. And we will continue to explore ways to strengthen our precautionary facilities and ensure that our programs are well designed. The Fund also actively contributes to addressing debt challenges. We provide technical support to individual restructuring, and working in conjunction with the World Bank, we are advancing work at the Global Debt Roundtable. And we are implementing the three-pillar approach to help countries with sustainable debt and strong reform agendas, but where high debt service crowds out productive spending. Simply put, the IMF will continue to help our members achieve economic and financial stability, both of which are prerequisites for reaching their development objectives. Excellencies, as we work together this week, the IMF will remain a trusted partner and champion of the international development agenda. Together, we can help bring our members towards a brighter future. Thank you and good morning.
I thank the Deputy Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund for his statement. I now invite Mr. Li Junhua, Secretary General of the Conference, to make a statement.

Your Majesty, the King and the Queen of Spain, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues, as the Secretary General of the Conference, it is a profound honor to welcome you all to the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. A profound gratitude goes to our host, the Government of Spain for its firm support and warm hospitality. This week marks a key moment in our effort to ensure every country, not just a privileged few, can mobilize resources necessary to build a just, inclusive and sustainable future. The global financing for development process has evolved over the past two decades. From the Monterrey Consensus to Doha Declaration, under the Addis Ababa Action Agenda, our journey has been anchored in multilateralism and solidarity. Each step was shaped by the realities of this time. Today, however, that framework is under profound stress. Global financing needs for developing countries to achieve SDGs now exceed $4.2 trillion annually, yet official development assistance remains stagnant or declining. At the same time, external debt servicing now consumes over 20% of the public revenues in many lower income countries. Climate finance commitment remained unfulfilled. In this fracture of the global landscape marked by the ongoing wars, economic fragmentation, heightened trade tensions, and declining trust in global institutions, our foundational commitments are being tested like never before. Excellencies, FFD4 offers us a once in a decade opportunity to shift the tide. The severe commitment is more than an outcome document. It is a new framework and a renewed global promise to mobilize finance at scale, to reform international financial architecture, and to put the people's need at the center of the development. This conference is the product of the sustained and inclusive efforts. The United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, UNDESA, has been honored to work alongside member states, UN system, and stakeholders at every step of this journey. Through the months of negotiations, member states have forged an impactful and action-oriented SEVIA commitment. As one minister put it during the negotiation, this is not about charity, this is about justice. fiscal justice, climate justice, and the generational justice. Through the genuine dialogue and exchange, we have the strength and the trust, broadened consensus, and the revived spirit of the multilateralism. Excellencies, Seville is not an end point. It is a launch pad for a new era of implementation, accountability and solidarity. UN DESA is ready to support Member States in translating the Seville commitment into tangible actions by tracking progress and ensuring transparency, by building national and institutional capacity, and by fostering continuous dialogue among all partners. We believe that This is not just about raising capital. It is about rebuilding trust, expanding opportunity, and empowering every country to shape its own sustainable future. Let us rise to this moment with unity, ambition, and shared determination to finance a better world for all. Thank you.

Your Majesties, distinguished Heads of State and Government, your Ministers, your Excellencies, we have heard the last speaker for the opening segment of the Conference. The six multi-stakeholder round tables will be chaired by two co-chairs and will be organized in accordance with the program of work of the conference and the modalities for the multi-stakeholder round tables approved by the preparatory committee. For Multi-Stakeholder Roundtable 2, His Excellency Mohammad Aurangzeb, Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue of Pakistan, and His Excellency Christopher McLennan, Deputy Minister of International Development and Global Affairs of Canada. For Multi-Stakeholder Roundtable 3, His Excellency K.P. Sharma Oli, Prime Minister of Nepal, and Her Excellency Ana Isabel Xavier, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and Cooperation and Vice Minister of State and Foreign Affairs of Portugal. For Multi-Stakeholder Roundtable 4, Her Excellency Nadia Fattah, Minister of Economy and Finance of Morocco, and Her Excellency Ms. Melita Gabric, Deputy Minister for Foreign and European Affairs and Minister for Development of Slovenia. For Multi-Stakeholder Roundtable 5, I have the honor of being one of the co-chairs together with His Excellency Bassirou Diomaye Diakaye, President of the Republic of Senegal. And for Multi-Stakeholder Roundtable 6, His Excellency Carlos Cuerpo Caballero, Minister of Economy, Commerce and Business of Spain, and His Excellency Sidi Keita, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of the Gambia. Before proceeding to approve the organization of work of the Conference, as set out in document A/CONF.227/2025/3, As outlined in a letter dated the 25th of June, 2025 addressed to all member states by the permanent representative of Spain to the United Nations in New York, I propose orally to revise the organization of work to proceed with the adoption of the civil commitment by beginning the consideration of agenda item 10, adoption of the outcome document of the conference this morning just before agenda item eight, which is the general debate. As outlined in the same letter, I also propose that any statements in explanation of vote that states may wish to deliver in connection with the adoption of the draft outcome document should be made as originally scheduled in the afternoon of Thursday, the 3rd of July. With that rather lengthy introduction, may I take it that the Conference wishes to approve the organization of work as set out in the aforementioned document A/CONF.227/2025/3 with the oral revisions that I have proposed? If there are no objections, then it is so decided. The Conference has thus concluded this stage of its consideration of agenda item 6 and we move on to agenda item 7, which is entitled Credentials of representatives participating in the Conference, appointment of the members of the Credentials Committee. As you know, Rule four of the rules of procedure provides that there shall be a credentials committee of nine members appointed at the beginning of the conference and that its composition shall be based on that of the credentials committee of the General Assembly of the United Nations at its 79th session. The following states are members of the credentials committee of the 79th session of the General Assembly. Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, China, Dominica, the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Liberia, Monaco, the Russian Federation and the United States of America. I have been informed by the Secretariat that Dominica and the United States of America have indicated that they will not be able to participate in the conference and accordingly they are not available to serve on the Credentials Committee. Therefore, in accordance with the past practice of the United Nations conferences, Canada from Western European and other States and Trinidad and Tobago from Latin American and Caribbean States have been nominated to replace the United States and Dominica respectively as members of the Credentials Committee. May I therefore take it that the Conference wishes to appoint Antigua and Barbuda, Cape Verde, Canada, China, the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Liberia, Monaco, the Russian Federation and Trinidad and Tobago as members of the Credentials Committee of the Conference? I hear no objection. It is therefore so decided. Delegates are reminded that, in accordance with the Rules of Procedure of the Conference, credentials issued by the head of state or government or by the minister of foreign affairs or in the case of the European Union by the president of the European Commission should be submitted to the secretary general of the United Nations if they have not already been submitted. The conference has thus concluded its consideration, Your Excellencies, of sub-item A of agenda item seven. Distinguished Heads of State and Government, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the Conference will now proceed to consider agenda item 10, which is entitled Adoption of the outcome document of the Conference. The Conference has before it a draft resolution contained in document A/CONF.227/2025/Rev.1. entitled Seville Commitment, as recommended by the Preparatory Committee at its closing meeting on the 17th of June. I would like at this point to thank all States for their constructive participation in the negotiations on the Seville Commitment. Particular thanks are due to the co-chairs of the Preparatory Committee, His Excellency Zeferine Maniratanga, Permanent Representative of the Republic of Burundi to the United Nations in New York, and His Excellency Rui Vinas, Permanent Representative of Portugal to the United Nations in New York. I would like to thank them for guiding the work of the Preparatory Committee. And I'd also like to thank the co-facilitators of the intergovernmental negotiations, Ambassador Alicia Buendrostro Masieu, Deputy Permanent Representative of Mexico, Ambassador Lok Bahadur Tapa, Permanent Representative of Nepal, Ambassador Merete Fjeld Bratstad, Permanent Representative of Norway, and Ambassador Chola Milambo, Permanent Representative of Gambia to the United Nations in New York for leading and successfully concluding the negotiations on the draft outcome document in New York. In addition to bearing witness to this extraordinary success, I would now like to ask if the Conference would like to adopt the Seville Commitment as is contained in document A/CONF.227/2025/L/1. If there are no objections, it is so decided.

As previously agreed, we will now hear statements in explanation of vote at the closing meeting on the 3rd of July. The conference has thus concluded this stage of its consideration of agenda item 10. So the opening section has finished, and before beginning the general debate, I would like I beg your pardon. In accordance with the organization of work of the conference, statements in the general debate should not exceed five minutes, and we'd like to really ask you to respect that, although some flexibility will be given to statements on behalf of groups. Speakers with longer statements are encouraged to read a shorter version of their text and to submit the full length of their statement for posting in the journal of the United Nations. And in order to assist speakers in managing their time, a timer will be projected on the screen.
