I now have the honor of inviting our first speaker, His Excellency Abdul Latif Jamal Rashid, President of the Republic of Iraq.

Mr. President, I am pleased to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group 77 and China. Let me begin by extending our gratitude to His Majesty the King. the government and the people of Spain for hosting this historic conference and for the warm hospitality extended to our delegations. It is a privilege to gather here to reaffirm our commitment to multilateralism and global partnership on financing sustainable development. The Group of 77 and China wish to express a sincere appreciation to the co-chairs of the Preparatory Committee and the core facilitators for their leadership throughout this complex process. We also appreciate their efforts to ensure that the process remains inclusive and transparent. Mr. President, this conference is being held at an official -- at a critical juncture with those than five years to achieve the sustainable development goals. The world remains off the track to achieving the ambitious agenda we committed to it in 2015. The financing gap continued to widen and the challenges confronting the global south have become more urgent, demanding coordinated international action and renewed political will. Against this backdrop, the Group of 77 and China welcomes the adoption of outcome documents by consensus. We support this document as a balanced, constructive and forward-looking framework that reflects the collective aspirations to scale up efforts in mobilizing financing for sustainable development, especially in developing countries. The outcome reflects the group's shared commitment to solidarity and cooperation. It must serve as a foundation to address the systematic imbalances in the global and economical financial system. and to ensure that the voices and priorities of developing countries are heard. Mr. President, Group of 77 and China reiterates the centrality of North-South cooperation as the foundation of international development. We emphasize the importance of fulfilling all official development assistance commitments. and of providing adequate finance to developing countries in the line which their national priorities. At the same time, we reaffirm the value of South and South cooperation as a compliment to North-South cooperation, guided by the principle of mutual respect and non-conditionality. We believe in strengthening domestic resources, mobilizations of sustainable development. We must improve the international tax system, scale up foreign direct investments, lower remittance costs, challenge provide investment, reform the international financial architecture, ensure first ensure fair representations of developing countries in the international financial institutions, and eliminate all unilateral economic, financial, or trade measures against developing countries. We must also expand access to technology, capacity building, and long-term financing. The civil commitment can serve as a good basis for all to deliver the equality and quantity of the funding to accelerate sustainable development. We must continue to focus on those furthest behind and ensure that we live up to our commitment to leave no one or country behind. If one of us fail to achieve the agenda, we all fail. Moving forward, effective implementation of commitments is key. Let us also work to strengthen the role of the United Nations in the follow-up and review process in order to guarantee that financing for the development agenda is fair and inclusive. Let us use this conference to renew our collective efforts to achieve sustainable development goals by 2030. Because the challenges we face transcend national borders, no single country can achieve the SDGs alone. It calls for a shared vision, unified action, and global cooperation, promises should turn into action. Together, we can help a global financial architecture that serves the interests of all, not the few. The Group of 77 and China stands ready to engage with all the partners to ensure that financing for development becomes a true engine for sustainable and equitable progress. I would now like to deliver a statement in my national capacity.

In the name of God, most compassionate. Your Majesty, Your Excellencies, heads of governments, states, and international organizations, ladies and gentlemen, peace be upon you. I would like to thank His Excellency Prime Minister of Spain, Mr. Pedro Sanchez, for hosting this conference. I would like to thank Spain for ensuring the success of the conference. I would like also to express my gratitude to His Excellency, U.N. Secretary General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, for inviting us to take part in this very important conference. Ladies and gentlemen, This conference is taking place amidst very complex international and regional conditions, namely in the Middle East. They are also having an impact on the development process and hampering socioeconomic plans, namely in developing countries. We are encouraged to support the success of this important conference to achieve its goals, to achieve progress and development and economic reform, and this will have an impact on all the peoples of the world. Achieving these objectives at the international level should also be preceded by achievements at the national level.

We have seen how there were different challenges that were tackled as well as wars and economic embargoes and random plans which gave rise to lags in our development policy We have also established a development plan based on a balanced approach. This is particularly true after what we inherited from the various dictatorships. We are witnessing nowadays development at many different levels and we need cooperation from the international community in order to enhance our reconstruction plan and improve the living conditions of the people of Iraq. After having liberated Iraq from ISIS, the terrorist organization, our government launched the five-year development plan for 2024, 2028, and linked it to the SDGs. And we have succeeded for the first time in 37 years. We organized a population and housing census. last year, and we have also started improving public services and infrastructure and developed many critical plans, as well as working on empowering our population, women, and youths. When it comes to climate and environment, it's a very important sector for us, and we have adopted many policies such as integrating renewable energies as part of our infrastructure and agriculture and combating desertification and drought. We have also many partnerships with international organizations and we are cooperating with UN agencies in various sectors. Lately, Iraq has been able to preside the G77 in China.

We have also restored our very important role in terms of development. Our government has worked on promoting governance, administrative reform by supporting our statistics organizations based on the principles of transparency and namely in terms of managing of our resources. Ladies and gentlemen, Iraq still has a long journey to engage in order to achieve SDGs in 2030. And there are many challenges we are facing, such as huge reliance on oil as a main source of national income. That's why our economy is facing vulnerabilities in the face of changing and volatile prices in the international oil market. We also face numerous climate and environmental challenges. Uh, increasing, uh, temperatures to record levels, uh, reduced, uh, rainfalls, as well as the, uh, challenges. linked to desertification, dust storms, and the weak irrigation infrastructure. We also face challenges in terms of demographics and social conditions. We are facing a rapid demographic growth that requires the provision of employment, housing, reducing poverty and unemployment among the youth. In order to counter all these challenges, our government has launched many reforms in order to increase our chances to achieve success in achieving SDGs. We have our own agenda for development for 2030 and we included it in our five-year development plan for 2024-2028. Finally, We look forward to the support by the international community, UN, and other relevant organization in order to achieve our development goals, SDGs. We are a promising economic environment for countries, for companies that wish to invest in Iraq. We wish your conference success for the service of all the peoples of the world.

I thank the President of the Republic of Iraq. And I now have the honor of inviting His Excellency, Jao Manuel Gonzalez Lorenzo, President of the Republic of Angola, to speak on behalf of the Group of African States.

His Excellency Pedro Sanchez, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Spain. Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, His Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is a great honor for me to be present at this event in my capacity as Chairperson of the African Union, attended by distinguished figures from the UN member states. and the Kingdom of Spain, whom I greet on the occasion of this fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, which I consider to be a crucial opportunity for us to discuss ways to truly assist the developing countries in overcoming the limitations and constraints they face in order to foster progress and development. When the decision was made to convene this conference, nothing could have made us foresee that the world would experience such a turbulent time marked by uncertainties and threats that may undermine our expectations regarding development to which we are all committed as it is a crucial matter for the present and future of humanity. In the face of this most troubling scenario, the issue of peace and global security once again plays a central role in our discussions, without which we will not be able to make any progress towards our fundamental objectives as enshrined in the United Nations 2030 Agenda and the African Union 2063 Agenda. This evidence should lead us to acknowledge that only on the basis of reconciliation of interest and dialogue will we be able to build a broad understanding on global scale, which in our view is an imperative of our time so that we may, we do not move towards a catastrophe in which we would all stand to lose. After the end of the Cold War, when the world ought to have directed all its attention to economic and social development of our nations, we find ourselves once again witnessing the arms race, an unfortunate legacy of the previous century, which diverts substantial financial and scientific resources that should be dedicated to the service of education, teaching, youth training, scientific knowledge and research, all in the service of the main cause of development and well-being of peoples throughout the world. This is our perspective as African leaders who are deeply concerned about the direction that the world is taking, which demands from all of us a pusher of responsibility in addressing and seeking solutions to this alarming crisis that our planet is currently facing. Excellencies, we are gathered here to discuss development and the factors that contribute to the achievement of this goal. In this regard, this fourth conference represents an opportunity to give a dissasive impetus to initiatives that will enable us to find more agile and effective mechanism for mobilizing financial resources that allow us to confront the recurring challenges faced by developing countries such as climate shocks, fluctuation in commodity prices, erosion of confidence in the electoral system, and above all, the unsustainable burden of sovereign debt, which consumes more resources than those allocated to health and education combined, and drastically limits our capacity to finance our own development. This situation constitutes a clear obstacle to the achievement of the sustainable development goals of the 2030 agenda and the fulfillment of 2063 agenda, which express our shared commitment to building a fairer, more inclusive, and more resilient world. It is important to underscore that there will be no development on the African continent without solid and functional infrastructure. For we must acknowledge that the limited capacity for power production and transportation, the weak roads and highway network connecting our countries, the low investment in telecommunications and information technologies and other challenges of equivalent magnitude we face collectively represent factors that stifle economic growth and development as they gravely constrain trade and industry, the movement of people and goods, agriculture and job creation. It is in recognition of these realities that I've mentioned previously The African Union at its summit in February this year decided to convene a major conference under the theme infrastructure as a factor of development in Africa to be held in Angola in October this year. The purpose of the conference is to present to our international partners the mapping already undertaken of our needs in the area of public or public-private investment in infrastructure with the aim of attracting them and mobilizing resources for the realization of this great ambition which will yield considerable benefits and advantages for all parties involved in its implementation. Major investment in infrastructure in Africa require more appropriate financing model tailored to the economic conditions of African countries, which will entail restructuring of the current financial architecture so that it consistently takes into account Africa's priorities, which are often overlooked. In view of the foregoing facts, it is both fundamental and urgent. If we are to do justice to the concerns regarding the support for development of Africa, which are repeatedly raised in the various forum addressing this subject, that we should engage in profound reflection on the reforms required in the international financial system wherein those mostly need must have an active role and be included in the decision-making processes. Only with these conditions assured will it be possible to realize the goals set forth in the above mentioned development agendas, thereby preventing the sustainable development goals from becoming a merely declaration of good intentions, excellencies. To all that has been mentioned, we must add the issue of Africa's debt, which has a considerable negative impact on the implementation of our own programs, as it acts as a brake development due to the resulting scarcity of financial resources and limits our capacity to invest in key sectors of our economies with very adverse consequences for the social situation of the African countries. In view of this issue, we consider the Lome Declaration on Africa Debt adopted in May 2025 by the heads of state and government of the continent to be particularly timely as it represents an important milestone in the construction of an African common position. Within this framework, concrete proposals have been made in order to address the debt crisis, including amongst others, the creation of fairer and more transparent multilateral restructuring mechanism But to close us for the suspension of debt service in the event of external shocks and the encouragement of the use of local currency so as to reduce exposure to exchange rate risks. Excellencies, the African Union 2063 agenda aspires to transform Africa into an industrialized, integrated and economically sovereign continent, goals that are entirely attainable provided that all conditions that I've previously mentioned here are changed as they these indeed constitute the major bottlenecks to be overcome in order for us to achieve the goals that we've set for ourselves. Apart from the facts that I have mentioned, Africa possesses abundant natural resources to make the leap that is within its reach, thus contribute to the strengthening of the global economy and resolution of various crises that the world is facing. It is in this context that the Republic of Angola is resolutely committed to mobilizing internal resources, strengthening fiscal governance and fights against capital flight attaining great importance to the United Nations convention on international taxation whose negotiation have made encouraging progresses that might continue as this represents a historic opportunity to correct the balances of the global tax system and ensure equitable representation of developing countries in international tax decision-making processes. In parallel, I consider it appropriate to state that Africa continues to be one of the most vulnerable regions, yet paradoxically, one of the least responsible for greenhouse emissions. This reality should prompt the international community to accord the continent the attention it rightfully deserves by significantly increasing climate financing for adaptation and mitigation processes, supporting adjusted energy transition and providing incentives for debt conversion into concrete environmental actions, as we believe that climate resilience must go hand in hand with debt relief and the construction of sustainable economic models. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, The conference which is taking place in this beautiful city of Seville constitutes a crucial moment for reflection on issues relating to global sustainable development and for making decisions that may drive the implementation of the actions set forth in the African Union's 2063 Agenda. The idea of establishing a new financing model founded on economic justice and inclusion renders this conference a significant milestone in the transformation of perspectives upon which Africa may henceforth be provided with resources and necessary conditions to accelerate its transformation. I am confident that this conference will adopt decisions and make recommendations that will enable African countries to have a more streamlined access to sustainable investments and to financial transactions that would reduce the cost of indebtedness and contribute thus to strengthening their influence in the global financial governance. Thank you very much for your attention.

I thank the President of Angola and I now have the honour of inviting His Excellency Antonio Costa, President of the European Council, and Her Excellency Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, to speak on behalf of the European Union and its Member States.

President of the Government of Spain, dear Pedro, Secretary General, dear Antonio, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we will only achieve a world at peace if we bring about sustainable development. Ten years ago, the world adopted a commitment for its own future. the Sustainable Development Goals. Ten years on, we are still far from achieving those goals, largely because financing for development continues to be clearly insufficient. Today, from this podium, Ursula von der Leyen and I wish to send a loud and clear message The EU will continue the struggle. Together, we provide 42% of global official development aid, a total of 95 billion euros in 2023. It is believed that more than 300 billion euros in debt have been restructured thanks to the countries of the European Union that are part of the Paris Club. Our commitment stands firm. First of all, we are committed to reforming the international financial architecture, which has to be more inclusive and more effective and more representative. Secondly, we are committed to mobilizing new sources of financing as a matter of priority. And thirdly, we are supporting the common framework for of the G20. We have worked together in order to bring about the Seville commitment, which shows us the path to follow over the next few years, a path towards development which will not depend solely on the quantity but also the quality of aid mechanisms, one that will channel resources, both domestic and others, through greater tax collection. And it is a path that will involve the private sector more and which will pave the way towards optimizing the mechanisms for facing the debt challenge. A roadmap which aims ultimately to achieve a fairer international financial architecture that is more inclusive and better suited to the global challenges we face. multilateralism is not going through the best of times. That is true. But it is still alive, and today that is proof of it. And while we continue working together, it will remain alive. It is only together that we will be able to tackle climate change and poverty, inequalities, and build a lasting peace. The European Union will remain firmly committed by your side for our common future and our planet. All together, we will be stronger. Thank you.

Mr. President of the conference, Secretary General Guterres, what is that? Can this lectern please go down again? So, thank you, that is good. Be patient with me. Fantastic. Secretary General Guterres, presidents, prime ministers, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, let me start with a basic fact. Last year, development aid worldwide stood at just over $200 billion. The sustainable development goals annual investment gap, as Pedro Sanchez said, is in the trillions of dollars. To close this gap, we quite simply need a change of paradigm, new ways of mobilising much more finance. This is the core of the Compromisso de Sevilha that we agreed today, and it is exactly what Europe aims to deliver together with our global partners. Let me make three points in three minutes. How to make the most of public investment. The European Union provides 42% of the world's development aid. We're proud of this and our commitment is here to stay. At the same time, it is good that new donors are now stepping up. So why don't we combine forces, set up joint investment programmes that play on our respective strengths for maximum impact? This is the agreement we have just reached with India to invest together in third countries. And we will extend the same offer to other rising donors who share our goals. My second point, domestic taxation. This is the most sustainable source of funding for services like healthcare or education. And a fair tax system is vital to attract private investment. This is why we must bring to life the G20-OECD agreement on international corporate tax rules. This will bolster revenues in developing economies. And it is also a matter of fairness, because everyone should pay their fair share. My third and last point, we need the private sector. The private sector must get on board. And this is at the heart of Europe's Global Gateway investment program. We are attracting private capital in transformative development projects that create local growth and local jobs. In the first three years, Global Gateway has mobilized almost 180 billion euros in investment in our partner countries. Now we are on track to overshoot our initial target of 300 billion in seven years. And at the Global Gateway Forum in October in Brussels, we will announce further progress. So, to conclude, our message today is simple. Europe is ready to invest and to innovate. In these times of global uncertainty, you can count on us to support multilateralism. And to my good friend Ngozi, I listen very carefully to you. You have my full support to reform WTO. Thank you very much, and I wish us a successful conference.
I have the honor of inviting Her Excellency Iris Xiomara Castro Sarmiento, President of the Republic of Honduras, to address the conference.

Good morning. Heads of state and government, representatives of the United Nations, dear friends, I am the first woman in the history of Honduras, and I am convinced that we cannot speak of development unless we place financial equality and access to credit and gender equality at the very center of our efforts to achieve genuine global justice. I am speaking on behalf of a very brave people, one that belongs to one of the regions that has been the most battered in history. political instability, conflicts, and the imposition of a model of privatization that was dictated by international organizations, international credit organizations, and private banks, and which left us with poverty, corruption, and violence, as well as serious fiscal constraints which hamper our investment in our development. The president of the previous regime, Mr. Hernandez, who today has been sentenced in New York to 40 years of imprisonment, for 12 years and seven months he presided over a narco dictatorship with the assistance of foreign actors and he dismantled the productive base of our country. He granted privileges to major corporations and he exempted the most powerful from paying their taxes. At the same time, he turned away completely from micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Today in Honduras, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises provide eight out of ten jobs, yet their access to credit is almost non-existent, and when they do secure access to credit, they have to pay unfair, high rates. This neoliberal model, which we inherited, has left us with a 17 percent ratio of tax to GDP. which is far below the Latin American average and less than half the level that is recommended by the OECD. Inequality runs deep. Ten families with 25 economic groups have taken over 85% of our GDP and they pay merely 0.003% in taxes whereas the poorest pay up to 50%. They also control more than 40% of bank loans and they get preferential rates. Meanwhile, small companies can barely access 0.04% of credit, and they do so at very high interest rates. Over the last three and a half years since I took up office, we have started to dismantle this perverse system. We are eliminating the corrupt private banking systems and we have released vast ways of our territory from speculative capital which had been established prior to the coup d'etat. Two years ago, I submitted a bill to Congress on tax justice to try and establish the principle of global income and to try and force the most powerful among us to pay their taxes. But the members of parliament from the traditional parties who serve the financial oligarchy refused categorically to approve the bill. And despite all this, we have achieved something. We have managed to reactivate the agricultural bank which had been inactive for years. It is now providing fair loans to small producers. Almost one million peasants now receive fertilizers and improved seeds. and more than 66,000 families have access to loans at low interest rates for housing and for their production. Today, with transparency and political will, we have achieved the highest levels of social investment and investment in infrastructure and energy and the environment and security in the history of our country. In this international forum, I must, however, mention another problem which is asphyxiating our countries, and that is the problem of foreign debt. According to the United Nations, almost half of humankind is living in countries that have to spend more on paying interest on their debt than they can invest in investment in healthcare or on climate change. And what is worse is that the debt crisis is concentrated in the poorest countries, whereas the capitalist system is robust and solvent, but it inflicts suffering in people's daily lives. The international financial system maintains our nations in a crisis that prevents us from investing and prevents us from addressing inherited social difficulties. Today, Global public debt is in excess of $100 billion, and our budgets are bleeding as we have to pay banks and multilateral lending organizations, leaving very little for our people. So I would like to make an urgent appeal. We need structural transformation of the global financial system. We need to eliminate the tax privileges and the disproportionate control of the powerful and to build a financing model that is based on justice and dignity. I am convinced that Financing for development must have peoples at its heart, and it must be based on democratic governance, fair taxation, climate justice, and human rights. We will not rest until we achieve financial justice for development. I cannot but end by expressing my constant solidarity with the Palestinian people. Thank you.

I would like to thank the President of the Republic of Honduras, and I now have the honour of inviting His Excellency Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazwani, President of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, to address the conference.

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Excellencies, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Spain, His Excellency Secretary General of the United Nations Organization, ladies and gentlemen, I wish to begin by extending my most sincere gratitude to His Excellency Mr. Pedro Sanchez, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Spain, for his kind invitation and for the care and the kindness that he has extended on the basis of the robust ties linking our fraternal nations. I also wish to extend my gratitude to His Excellency Mr. Antio Khaterish, as well as all specialized organizations of the United Nations for the commendable efforts that they have been undertaking to implement the Addis Ababa 2015 program of action, as well as the commitments that have been undertaken through the Pact for the Future in 2024, particularly vis-a-vis The promotion of the spirit of partnership and solidarity and enhancement of multilateral cooperation in order to establish a conducive environment for sustainable development and to reform the financial, international financial governance system. This is geared towards finding the most effective means for the financing of development in a most effective, equitable and sustainable way. This finance for the financing for development conference represents an opportunity for us to achieve meaningful progress progress which our developing countries and the entire world need now more than ever before in the light of the magnitude of the challenges obstructing the development process for comprehensive global and balanced sustainable development. Ladies and gentlemen, poverty and the vulnerabilities buffeting our world, specifically developing countries, and the weakness of institutions, lack of access to basic services, heightened violence and terrorism, the proliferation of hotbeds of tension and war, and the deterioration of the environment throughout the planet are all clear signs of a lack of hope when it comes to the achievement of SDGs. within the established timeline if the current approach is maintained. In order to achieve the SDGs, there is a need to mobilize tremendous resources. There is a need to provide equitable ease of access to them. For this reason, our country, like many developing countries, has undertaken Herculean efforts as we seek to mobilize national resource by classifying the majority of activities in parallel sectors by enhancing digitization of the economy, as well as we seeking to promote the private sector and to promote the development of the market while improving fiscal governance. However, resources that developing countries are in a position to mobilize themselves are high, but they do not cover but a fraction of their growing development needs. And this makes it necessary for them to bridge this gap and to meet these needs. And therefore, they need to be able to count on external financing, which unfortunately is in short supply, and access to this is uneven. Most developing countries, therefore, have undertaken to establish the necessary conditions to attract external and foreign investment. And this includes the establishment of -- this includes the enhancement of rule of law, greater transparency, combating corruption, as well as improving the business climate while at the same time generating numerous promising investment opportunities. And yet, the development financing mechanisms within the international financial system as it currently stands insufficient, and day after day, the ability of these countries to effectively address the growing need for resources for balanced, sustainable development, with each passing day, this becomes all the more clear. Global GDP, when it comes to official development assistance and global GDP remains, falls short of the 0.7 percent goal which has been agreed to at the international level. The debt issue continues to worsen, and the issue of access to credit remains uneven, and it is neither equitable nor balanced. It is clear that development cannot be achieved in developing countries unless -- if these countries continue to spend more for debt servicing and repayment of debts than for health care and basic services provision. This is a significant -- the cost of this is significantly higher for developing countries than developed countries. A multilateral cooperation is a sine qua non here. This cooperation needs to be established in order to renew trust and solidarity among peoples and countries to find solutions to bridge the development financing gap. While reforming international financing governance, we need to adopt innovative financing mechanisms and to build robust partnerships to tackle the growing difficulties of the global development landscape in order to offset the declining opportunities of traditional financing. All of this is a part of our collective responsibility to a shared future and our crucial need to extricate our planet from this infernal cycle. For this reason, we in the Islamic Republic of Mauritania reiterate our full report to the results of the fourth Financing for Development Conference and our desire to contribute to implementation of the recommendations thereof. Thank you.

I would like to kindly remind all our speakers that the speaking time for statements during the general debate is limited to five minutes. And I would like to thank the President of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. And now I have the honour of inviting His Excellency, Alar Karis, President of the Republic of Estonia, to address the conference.

Honourable UN Secretary-General Guterres, President of the Conference, esteemed organisers, dear colleagues. In the 10 years following the Addis Ababa Action Agenda, the development landscape has changed a lot. We are facing a growing number of challenges which are reducing the resource available for development financing. Recent shocks, including more frequent catastrophic climate events, trade tensions and growing debt burden, U-turns in national development policies, Russia's aggression against Ukraine, war unleashed in wider Middle East and other deep frozen conflicts have tightened global financing conditions and hindered, if not reversed, our progress towards the sustainable development goals. Therefore, it is pertinent to ask what shall we do more, differently or better to overcome this? Ladies and gentlemen, It is clear that sustainable development and its financing require cooperation between governments, international organizations, the private and non-profit sectors, and civil society. The challenges can be overcome if everyone makes an effort and works together. We must be realistic and goal-oriented in our reforms. be more inclusive, including breaking development ceilings, for example, in middle-income countries. National ownership of one's own future is crucial. This includes strong domestic policy and reforms that enable development, increasing domestic resource mobilization, improving efficiency of public spending and absorption capacity, strengthening debt management, data transparency, holding corruption, and last but not least, improving democratic and human centred governance. We can accelerate the development agenda by digitalisation and harnessing artificial intelligence. but also by better access to financial services and economic empowerment of women. It is also important to involve private entities and financial institutions, including foreign capital, as their role has increased in channeling resources into sustainable economic activities. Investments in sustainable technologies and companies that adhere to social and economical standards will help us achieve the SDGs. Digitization of state services is one important accelerator of reform and effectiveness of governance. That is where public-private partnership has a potential to provide solutions. Estonia has a e-governance technology and platform and well-known track record of joint work on bilateral level with other nations and with international development institutions to this end. And we are more than willing to continue that endeavor. In addition, it is important to improve understanding of the importance of an awareness of financial and finance in sustainable development. Investments are a financial decision, but also a valuable activity that supports the creation of our common sustainable future. To achieve this, It is necessary to create clear rules, but also use existing ones where needed, provide new incentives to encourage both local and foreign companies and individuals to contribute. It is also important to strengthen financial instruments such as green bonds and sustainable development funds. These financial instruments allow for the raising of capital and its responsible and efficient channeling. There must also be a clear system of metrics and reporting to help monitor the impact of financing and ensure that resources are indeed used for their intended purposes. To conclude, financing sustainable development requires innovation, collaboration, and commitment. If we can invest wisely and responsibly, we can create a better future for our planet, society, and economy. Let me reiterate that Estonia is and will be a reliable and solid donor. Estonia's strength, education, and digital development are domains in which we share our 35 years of reform experience. To bring that forward, Estonia also pledges the upgrade of our COVSTACK initiative through the Seville Platform for Action. Let us move forward together, confident that sustainable development is possible and it includes everyone. The outcome document, Compromisso de Seville, shall be brought into action. Thank you very much for your attention.
I would like to thank the President of the Republic of Estonia and I now have the honour to invite Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique to address the conference.

Thank you.

Your Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Your Excellency, the President-elect of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, Your Excellency, Mr. President of the Government of Spain, Your Excellency, Denis Francis, President of the 79th session of the General Assembly of the United Nations, your excellencies, heads of states and governments here present, esteemed representatives from various organizations, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen. It is with great honor and a deep sense of responsibility that Mozambique stands before you in this global conference here in Seville. dedicated on financing for development, we applaud the approval of the Seville commitment. This conference offers a strategic opportunity to reflect on effective, innovative, and sustainable solutions for the challenges that the countries in the global south are grappling with. and we reaffirm the value of multilateral cooperation for the realization of the U.N. Agenda 2030. Mozambique has enjoyed remarkable economic growth over the past two decades. However, internal and external recent shocks, such as terrorism in the north of the country, especially in some districts of the province of Cabo Delgado, Extreme climatic events like floods, cyclones, due to our geographical location, have caused social hardships that have slowed our economy, reducing employment, especially for the youth, food security, and the state's capacity to finance vital sectors such as healthcare, education, and infrastructure. In spite of this pressing situation, we are strengthening our commitment to structural reforms guided by a clear vision towards economic transformation embodied in our national development strategy, 2025-2044, consisting of five intertwined pillars, namely good governance, strategic infrastructure, industrialization, human capital, and environmental sustainability. This vision is well aligned with the central principle of this conference, which has to do with the urgency for a more inclusive global financial architecture that provides developing countries better access to financing and more equitable opportunities. At the domestic level, we prioritize the expansion of the taxing basis and modernization of the fiscal system with special focus on digital taxation, review of fiscal benefits and control of natural resources export. We are also implementing a national strategy for climate financing as to transform Mozambique into a regional green financing by 2035. We commend this conference for placing emphasis on innovative instruments such as the blended finance and underscore the urgent need for strengthening national development banks with catalytic platforms for investment in industrialization, including small to medium enterprises and the sector of agriculture as the basis for development. Ladies and gentlemen, based on this vision, Mozambique wishes to present a concise set of strategic proposals that are aligned with the expected outcomes of this conference. One, a new results-based global partnership for climate finance focusing on highly vulnerable countries with low emission of carbon and adaptation projects, creation of national and regional development banks to finance industrialization in rural areas, small to medium enterprises and green economy, continental platform for digital financial inclusion focusing on youth and women initiatives to promote access to micro investments through African fintechs, multilateral mechanism for debt sustainability management with guidelines on transparency and incentives to investment in strategic sectors, global compact for human capital development with regional centers of excellence in energy transition, agro industry and digital governance. These proposals are just, are not just national solutions. They are a call for concerted global action. We need a new model for cooperation that places climate finance, inclusive industrialization and strategic capacity building at the center of the global priorities. Mozambique affirms its commitment not to leave anyone behind and calls for a new international financial architecture that embraces the African challenges not as mere limitations but as opportunities for shared transformation. Thank you for your attention. Let us work. I thank you.

I thank the President of the Republic of Mozambique for his statement. I now have the honor to invite His Excellency William Ruto, Head of State and Government of the Republic of Kenya, to address the conference.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I address this fourth Financing for Development Summit at a defining moment for global cooperation. The agreed outcome document signals a renewed, if not hard-won, commitment to multilateralism and equitable development. I welcome its emphasis on national ownership and sovereignty, For those of us from Africa, Africa's development is first, our foremost responsibility. We approach it with purpose and determination. Yet strong global partnerships remain essential to our collective success. Calls for greater flexibility in ODA are steps in the right direction. I am encouraged by the recognition of trade and industrialization as drivers of structural transformation. No country has achieved lasting prosperity without manufacturing and export diversification. Africa is ready, poised and prepared to become the next frontier of global production and innovation. I also welcome the focus on debt liquidity and the cost of capital. There is now consensus on the need for a development-oriented sovereign debt architecture, where public debt is an instrument for development, not a trap for distress. Additionally, effective debt management and crisis prevention, including Debt transparency and responsible borrowing and lending are key, while lowering borrowing costs and expanding fiscal space is essential for sustainable development. It is imperative to have debt sustainability and credit assessments that are accurate, objective, and long-term oriented. The independent expert review on debt, nature and climate, Kenya co-led with Colombia, France and Germany, exemplifies meaningful partnership for inclusive and sustainable growth. The outcome document also supports the global financing safety net, emphasizing governance reform at the IMF and mechanisms to facilitate easier access to precautionary instruments, lower lending rates, and better use of SDRs. The inclusion of SDRs rechanneling, support for capital adequacy framework and efforts to incorporate multidimensional vulnerability into financial access signals real progress. What was once radical is now becoming mainstream. We finally have consensus, ladies and gentlemen, on reforming the international financial architecture. This outcome document now calls for strengthening global economic governance by enhancing the voice and representation of developing countries in international financial institutions. Let us be clear, without affordable capital and open markets, progress will stall. High debt premiums cannot be fixed by technical adjustments alone. Credit rating agencies also need to change their understanding of African economies. The Africa Credit Rating Agency is a crucial step in gaining a better understanding of Africa. Africa's role is critical to the global climate agenda, but we cannot deliver if our goods, services, and carbon credits are excluded from the global markets or if entire value chains are blocked. We must design trade rules and pricing systems that reward green production and accelerate decarbonization. Africa must be part of that solution, transforming green premiums into green discounts. While I respect the document structure, from domestic to global resources, let us not confuse form with priority. Public international finance remains indispensable. Africa is not asking for favours. We are asking for fairness, partnership, and investment. I urge the United States of America to reconsider its position. and call on other member states with reservations on parts of this consensus to fully support the outcome document. The world's and Africa's futures are inseparable. Together, let us walk this path with honesty, urgency, and resolve. Kenya certainly will, and I thank you.
I thank the head of state and government of Kenya, and it is my honor now to invite his excellency, Jose Maria Pereira Neves, president of the Republic of Cabo Verde, to address the conference.

Ladies and gentlemen, heads of state and government, distinguished delegates, I welcome the adoption of the Seville Commitment, which can become an operational tool for transformation, provided that This is supported and underpinned by robust, measurable and appropriately financed commitments. We are living in an era of historic need. The annual deficit of $4 billion in the financing of the Sustainable Development Goals is not merely a figure. This is a global alarm. This reflects the structural asymmetries within the international financial architecture, which continue to penalize developing countries, in particular, small island developing states. Cabo Verde is well aware of these limitations, We have reformed our public finances. We have broadened the tax base in an equitable way. We have digitized the processes and we have aligned our budgetary policies with the SDGs. And yet no degree of internal rigor can compensate for the systematic constraints of a system that remains inaccessible to many, inequitable, and unadapted to meeting our present-day realities. The small island developing countries are facing a three-pronged structural challenge: heightened debt, which reduces the fiscal space; a fragile economic base that is vulnerable to external shocks and institutional constraints which constrain the efficiency of public and governmental expenditures. With less than .003 percent of global emissions, Cabo Verde is buffeted by the disproportionate consequences of climate change. With resources at our disposal that fall short of what is necessary to tackle this challenge and rebuild, we stress the urgent need for additional predictable and adaptation-targeted climate financing, particularly in the areas of renewable energies, coastal protection, water management, and sustainability of the oceans. We support the Antigua and Barbuda agenda for small island developing countries. The commitments need to be accompanied by effective and efficient and accessible tools, green and blue funds, sustainable debt investment exchanges, and greater technical assistance for the most vulnerable states. We applaud the adoption of the multidimensional vulnerability index for the United Nations, and we call for the full and comprehensive adaptation thereof by international financial institutions. We advocate more equitable representation of small and developing states within the global economic and financial decision-making bodies. The meaningful presence of our countries in executive boards and technical bodies of multilateral institutions is crucial to building a genuinely inclusive and development-focused architecture. Moreover, there is an urgent need to scale up internal resource mobilization with modern, progressive, and digitized fiscal systems, while at the same time supporting the private sector, small and medium-sized enterprises, and youth entrepreneurship. The FFD4 should not be another promise postponed. This needs to be the start of a new cycle of consistency, of shared responsibility and of global solidarity. Cabo Verde stands ready to shoulder this commitment. with a strong voice and a constructive contribution, because without fiscal justice, there is no global equity. Without equitable financing, there is no real transformation. And without inclusion, development will forever remain incomplete. Thank you.
I thank the President of Cabo Verde. It is my honor now to invite Her Excellency Gordana Siljanovska Davkova, President of the Republic of North Macedonia, to address the conference.

Thank you.

Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I wish to extend my heartfelt gratitude to our Spanish hosts for organizing this fourth International Conference on Financing for Development in Seville. Eighty years ago, The United Nations rose from the ruins of the world toward the second to prevent future wars and colonialism, uphold human rights, advance justice and international law, and unite nations behind global efforts like the Paris Agreement and the Sustainable Development Goals. 80 years on, Many of these achievements are unfortunately being undermined by geopolitical rivalry, economic fragmentation, and systemic risks. The multilateral efforts to implement the SDGs and address the pressing global challenges of poverty, inequality, climate change, and injustice are often being considered a Don Quixotic mission. Just as Don Quixote faces misunderstanding and resistance, the sustainable development movement encounters geopolitical and geo-economic challenges. Despite these setbacks, we believe that a better world is possible, even if the path is difficult. To revitalize the UN and strengthen the multilateral system, we adopted the Pact for the Future as a new global Rousseauian social contract. At the core of every social contract lies a fundamental truth that all parties share a responsibility not just to uphold their rights, but also their duty to care for the system. This is an ambitious document which is a landmark in our collective quest for more innovative, more united and more effective development. But it's not enough just to state our ambition. Making headway on the path towards united sustainable development requires action. First, the reform of global economic governance to correct the systemic inequalities that exist. These continue to hamper our domestic attempts to achieve development and that is why we support the Seville Outcome document calling for a more inclusive, more equitable global economic governance. This includes greater participation of countries of the South in decision-making in the Bretton Woods institutions, notably the World Bank and the IMF. Secondly, it is critical that we continue reforming international taxation so that we can more effectively combat tax evasion and illicit financial flows, we need to strengthen transparency and ensure that wealth is taxed where it is created, that is to say where companies do business. Thirdly, The issue of debt warrants particular attention. For us, it is of absolute priority as it has a massive impact on our overall economy. Senegal calls for a review of the criteria used by the credit rating agencies to bear in mind the effects on countries' ability to access credit. We need to have a fairer, more inclusive, more predictable system with automatic suspension clauses should shocks occur. What is laid out in the civil outcome document sends a positive sign and we need to work on this to help us to mobilize financing for development.
